## 8. The degree monoid of a frame

### 8.1 Graded reflection

**Definition 8.1.** The *$k$-fold reflection axiom* is $C_k(p) := \Box^k p \to p$. For $k=1$ it is the reflection axiom; for $k = 0$ it is a tautology.

Write $R^k$ for the $k$-step reachability relation: $w R^k v$ iff there is a walk $w = x_0 R x_1 R \cdots R x_k = v$.

**Theorem 8.2.** $C_k(p)$ is valid on $F$ iff every world lies on a closed walk of length exactly $k$, i.e. $w R^k w$ for all $w$.

*Proof sketch.* If every world lies on such a walk, then $\Box^k p$ at $w$ delivers $p$ at $w$. Conversely, take $V(p) := \{x : w R^k x\}$; then $\Box^k p$ holds at $w$ by construction, so validity gives $w \in V(p)$, i.e. $wR^kw$. For $k=1$ this recovers Theorem 3.1. $\square$

**Definition 8.3 (Degree monoid).** $D(F) := \{k \in \mathbb{N} : F \models \Box^k p \to p\}$.

**Theorem 8.4.** $D(F)$ is an additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$.

*Proof.* $0 \in D(F)$ since $C_0$ is a tautology (the empty walk). If $j,k \in D(F)$ and $w$ is any world, concatenate a closed $j$-walk at $w$ with a closed $k$-walk at $w$ to obtain a closed $(j+k)$-walk; by Theorem 8.2, $j+k \in D(F)$. $\square$

### 8.2 Values realised

**Theorem 8.5 (Löb frames).** If $F$ is nonempty and validates the Löb axiom, then $D(F) = \{0\}$.

*Proof sketch.* A closed walk of positive length in a transitive relation yields $wRw$, contradicting Corollary 4.7. $\square$

**Theorem 8.6 (Equality frames).** If each world sees exactly itself then $D(F) = \mathbb{N}$: every world has closed walks of every length. $\square$

**Theorem 8.7 (Cycle frames).** For the directed $n$-cycle $Z_n$ ($n \ge 1$), $D(Z_n) = n\mathbb{N}$: closed walks exist exactly in lengths divisible by $n$. $\square$

**Theorem 8.8 (Non-principality).** Let $K_3$ be the three-world frame in which each world sees the other two and not itself. Then
$$D(K_3) = \{k : k \ne 1\} = \{0,2,3,4,5,\dots\} = \langle 2,3\rangle,$$
and there is no $d$ with $D(K_3) = d\mathbb{N}$.

*Proof sketch.* There is no closed walk of length $1$, since no world sees itself. There is one of length $2$ (out and back) and one of length $3$ (around the triangle); every $k \ge 4$ is $2a+3b$ for nonnegative integers $a, b$, so Theorem 8.4 supplies all remaining degrees. If $D(K_3) = d\mathbb{N}$, then $d \mid 2$ and $d \mid 3$, so $d = 1$ and $1 \in D(K_3)$, a contradiction. $\square$

**Remark 8.9.** Theorem 8.8 refutes the natural conjecture that the graded soundness degrees of a frame are always the multiples of a fundamental period. The degree monoid is a genuine numerical-semigroup-valued invariant: the possible depths at which a structure "trusts itself" need not be closed under divisibility, only under addition.

---

## 9. Algorithms

Three procedures underlie the computational content of Sections 5–8.

**Algorithm A (Löb-validity check).** *Input:* a Boolean matrix $R$ of size $n$. *Output:* whether the corresponding frame validates the Löb axiom. Check $R_{aa} = 0$ for all $a$ and $R_{ab} \wedge R_{bc} \Rightarrow R_{ac}$ for all triples. Complexity $O(n^3)$ with bitset rows reducing it to $O(n^2)$ word operations. Correctness is Theorem 5.3. Note that a naive semantic check would cost $O(2^{n} \cdot n \cdot |\varphi|)$ per formula and would not even be well defined for infinite frames; the bridge is what makes the check finite.

**Algorithm B (Enumeration of labelled strict orders).** *Input:* $n$. *Output:* $\mathrm{L}(n)$, or the list of all Löb frames on $n$ worlds. Build up point by point: given a strict order $P$ on $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$, the extensions to $\{0,\dots,m\}$ are indexed by pairs $(D, U)$ where $D$ is a down-set of $P$, $U$ is an up-set of $P$, and every element of $D$ is below every element of $U$ in $P$. (These conditions are precisely what transitivity through the new point requires; they force $D \cap U = \emptyset$ and hence irreflexivity.) The cost is proportional to the number of orders produced times $4^{m}$ candidate pairs, vastly better than the $2^{n^2}$ of brute force: $\mathrm{L}(6) = 130023$ is reached in seconds where brute force would examine $6.9 \times 10^{10}$ matrices.

**Algorithm C (Degree monoid).** *Input:* a matrix $R$ and a bound $B$. *Output:* $D(F) \cap [0,B]$. Compute the reachability sets $R^k(w)$ by iterated Boolean matrix–vector products and test $w \in R^k(w)$ for all $w$. Complexity $O(B n^3)$ (or $O(Bn^2)$ words). By Theorem 8.4 the output determines $D(F)$ completely once the truncation contains a generating set — for instance once it contains two coprime values $j, k$, all integers $\ge (j-1)(k-1)$ are present.

---

## 10. Discussion

### 10.1 What the census measures

The equality $\mathrm{L}(n) = \#\{\text{labelled strict partial orders on } n \text{ points}\}$ is more than a coincidence of numbers: it is a translation of a second-order semantic condition into an order-theoretic one, licensed by Theorem 5.1 and made effective by Theorem 5.3. It gives a quantitative form to a qualitative slogan. "A theory may not assert its own soundness" becomes "reflexive and irreflexive frames do not meet"; "well-foundedness is a strong hypothesis" becomes "$19$ out of $512$, and $2^{-3n^2/4+o(n^2)}$ asymptotically".

### 10.2 The role of the finite collapse

The infinitary condition of converse well-foundedness is indispensable in general: the successor frame on $\mathbb{N}$ is transitive-free but irreflexive, and its transitive closure — the strict order $<$ on $\mathbb{N}$ — is transitive, irreflexive, and converse *ill*-founded, hence not a Löb frame. Irreflexivity plus transitivity is therefore genuinely weaker than the Löb condition over infinite carriers; the collapse of Theorem 5.1 is a finiteness phenomenon, and it is precisely the finiteness that makes the enumeration meaningful.

### 10.3 Definability has hard boundaries

The three closure principles of Corollary 7.7 are not technicalities: each is realised as an actual obstruction (Theorems 7.8–7.10). Modal validity is invariant under operations that preserve local visibility structure — surjective bounded images, disjoint unions — and any property not so invariant, however natural, is beyond axiomatic reach. Notably, this includes properties that all the frames of a definable class happen to have, such as irreflexivity for the Löb frames.

### 10.4 Degrees and semigroups

The degree monoid furnishes an unexpected point of contact with the theory of numerical semigroups. Theorem 8.8 shows the invariant is not merely a period, and raises the realisation problem: which submonoids of $\mathbb{N}$ arise? Since $D(F)$ is by Theorem 8.2 the intersection over all worlds of the closed-walk-length monoids of the digraph, the question is purely graph-theoretic, and known results about cycle-length sets in strongly connected digraphs are the natural tool.

---

## 11. Future directions

**C1. Realisation of degree monoids.** *Conjecture:* for every additive submonoid $S \le \mathbb{N}$ with $S \ne \{0\}$ and finite complement in the group it generates, there is a finite frame $F$ with $D(F) = S$; conversely every degree monoid of a finite frame is such a submonoid. The insight is that $D(F)$ is the set of $k$ such that *every* world lies on a closed walk of length $k$, so the realisation question concerns the intersection over vertices of the cycle-length monoids of a digraph — and the three-world complete irreflexive frame already shows this intersection can be the non-principal semigroup $\langle 2,3\rangle$, refuting the naive "always $d\mathbb{N}$" reading. Two extremes ($\{0\}$, $\mathbb{N}$) and two nontrivial values ($n\mathbb{N}$, $\langle 2,3\rangle$) are established, so the general problem can be attacked with the closed-walk concatenation machinery already in hand.

**C2. A Goldblatt–Thomason theorem for these frame classes.** *Conjecture:* a class $\mathcal{C}$ of finite frames is the frame class of some modal system iff $\mathcal{C}$ is closed under surjective bounded morphic images, closed under and reflecting disjoint unions, and closed under generated subframes. The three closure directions are established here (Corollary 7.7), and they are strong enough to refute definability in three different ways (irreflexivity fails images, "some reflexive world" fails summands, non-emptiness fails the empty frame); the open half is the converse — building, from a closed class, an explicit system (for instance the validity system of $\mathcal{C}$) and proving its frame class is exactly $\mathcal{C}$. Theorem 7.12 is already a proof of the converse for one class, so the pattern "take the validity system of $\mathcal{C}$, show soundness for $\mathcal{C}$, and use a definability theorem for the reverse inclusion" is available for generalisation.

**C3. No modal shortcut for the counting sequence.** *Conjecture:* $\mathrm{L}(n) = 1, 1, 3, 19, 219, 4231, \dots$ is not expressible as $2^{q(n)}$ for a polynomial $q$, nor as any product of binomial coefficients; more sharply, for every fixed modal formula $\varphi$, the number of frames on $n$ labelled worlds validating $\varphi$ either has such a closed form or agrees with the labelled-poset sequence, with no intermediate growth rates achievable.

---

## 12. Conclusion

Frame definability is the hinge between the syntax of modal axioms and the combinatorics of directed graphs. Turning it carefully, we found that the axiom expressing Löb's theorem pins down exactly the transitive converse well-founded frames; that over a finite world set this is exactly strict partial order; that the resulting census of "Löbian universes" is the classical labelled-poset sequence $1, 1, 3, 19, 219, 4231, 130023, \dots$; that the rival axiom of internalised soundness admits $2^{n^2-n}$ frames and shares none of them; that three natural frame properties are provably beyond the expressive power of any axiom system; and that the graded degrees of self-trust form a numerical semigroup which need not be principal. On three worlds, the answer to the question with which we began is nineteen.

\begin{abstract}
We develop a correspondence theory between modal axioms and combinatorial conditions on Kripke accessibility relations, and use it to convert a question about provability logic into an exact enumeration problem. Our central bridge result is that a single instance of the L\"ob axiom $\Box(\Box p \to p) \to \Box p$, over one propositional variable, is valid on a frame precisely when its accessibility relation is transitive and converse well-founded, and that over a finite carrier this condition collapses to transitivity together with irreflexivity --- that is, to the frame relation being a strict partial order. Consequently the number of frames on $n$ labelled worlds validating the L\"ob axiom equals the number of labelled strict partial orders on $n$ points; we certify the initial values $1,1,3,19$ by exhaustive verification through the bridge, compute the continuation $219, 4231, 130023$ by an order-theoretic enumeration, and prove that the sequence is monotone by exhibiting an injection that adjoins an isolated world. Against this we place the exact count $2^{n^2-n}$ of frames validating the reflection axiom $\Box p \to p$: on three worlds, $64$ frames validate reflection and only $19$ validate L\"ob, while no nonempty frame validates both. We complement the positive correspondences ($T$, $4$, $D$, $B$, $5$, L\"ob, and the graded family $\Box^{k}p \to p$) with a transfer theory --- bounded morphisms and disjoint unions --- and three limitative theorems: irreflexivity, ``some world is reflexive'', universality and non-emptiness are each undefinable by any set of modal formulas, hence are not the sound-frame class of any proof system. Finally we introduce the \emph{degree monoid} of a frame, the additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ consisting of those $k$ for which $\Box^k p \to p$ is valid, and show that it is not always of the form $d\mathbb{N}$: the three-world complete irreflexive frame realises the numerical semigroup $\langle 2,3\rangle = \{0,2,3,4,\dots\}$.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}

\subsection{L\"ob's theorem and its frames}

Let $\Box$ be read as ``is provable in a fixed formal theory''. L\"ob's theorem states that if a theory proves $\Box p \to p$ then it proves $p$; internalised as a schema of the provability calculus it becomes the \emph{L\"ob axiom}
\[
  L:\qquad \Box(\Box p \to p) \to \Box p .
\]
Taking $p$ to be $\bot$ recovers G\"odel's second incompleteness theorem. In the semantic reading due to Kripke, $\Box$ quantifies over accessible worlds; the logic obtained by adding $L$ to the basic normal modal logic is sound and complete for the transitive converse well-founded frames.

The subject of this paper is the frame-theoretic content of this and neighbouring axioms, pushed as far as an exact enumeration. Our organising question is: how many Kripke frames on $n$ labelled worlds validate the L\"ob axiom, and how does that number compare with the number of frames validating the reflection (soundness) axiom?

\subsection{Contributions}
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \textbf{Correspondence theory} (\S3): each of $T$, $4$, $D$, $B$, $5$ defines its expected relational condition, using a \emph{single} instance over a \emph{single} propositional variable, with explicit witnessing valuations.
  \item \textbf{The L\"ob correspondence} (\S4): validity of one L\"ob instance is equivalent to transitivity plus converse well-foundedness; the second half is obtained from the maximal-element formulation, so no infinite descending sequence, and hence no dependent choice, is required.
  \item \textbf{The finite collapse and the bridge} (\S5): on a finite frame L\"ob validity is equivalent to strict partial orderhood, hence to a decidable matrix condition.
  \item \textbf{Enumeration} (\S6): the count $\Lcount(n)$ satisfies $\Lcount(0..6)=1,1,3,19,219,4231,130023$, is monotone, and is dwarfed by the reflexive count $2^{n^2-n}$.
  \item \textbf{Transfer and limitative theory} (\S7): a three-part closure package for the sound-frame class of any proof system, with three undefinability theorems.
  \item \textbf{The degree monoid} (\S8): $\Box^k p \to p$ defines ``every world lies on a closed walk of length $k$''; the valid degrees form an additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$ which need not be of the form $d\mathbb{N}$.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Preliminaries}

\subsection{Syntax}
Fix a set of propositional variables. \emph{Modal formulas} are generated by
\[
  \varphi ::= \bot \mid p \mid \varphi \to \varphi \mid \Box\varphi,
\]
with $\neg\varphi := \varphi\to\bot$ and $\Diamond\varphi := \neg\Box\neg\varphi$; $\Box^k\varphi$ is $\varphi$ prefixed by $k$ boxes, so $\Box^0\varphi=\varphi$. Three schemas recur: the \emph{reflection} instance $T(\varphi):=\Box\varphi\to\varphi$, the \emph{L\"ob} instance $L(\varphi):=\Box(\Box\varphi\to\varphi)\to\Box\varphi$, and the \emph{consistency formula} $\Con := \neg\Box\bot$.

\subsection{Frames, models, validity}

\begin{definition}[Frame]
A \emph{frame} $F$ is a pair $(W,R)$ with $W$ a set of \emph{worlds} and $R \subseteq W\times W$ the \emph{accessibility relation}. We write $wRv$ and say $w$ \emph{sees} $v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Valuation and satisfaction]
A \emph{valuation} assigns to each variable a subset of $W$. Satisfaction is defined by
\[
  F,V,w \not\models \bot; \qquad F,V,w \models p \iff w \in V(p);
\]
\[
  F,V,w \models \varphi\to\psi \iff \bigl(F,V,w\models\varphi \Rightarrow F,V,w\models\psi\bigr);
\]
\[
  F,V,w \models \Box\varphi \iff \forall v\,\bigl(wRv \Rightarrow F,V,v\models\varphi\bigr).
\]
Hence $F,V,w\models\Diamond\varphi$ iff some $v$ with $wRv$ satisfies $\varphi$, and $F,V,w\models\Con$ iff $w$ has a successor.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Validity, definability]
$\varphi$ is \emph{valid on} $F$, written $F\models\varphi$, if it is satisfied at every world under every valuation. A set $\Gamma$ \emph{defines} a class $\mathcal{C}$ of frames if for every $F$: $F\models\varphi$ for all $\varphi\in\Gamma$ iff $F\in\mathcal{C}$. For a single formula this reads: $\{\varphi\}$ defines $\mathcal{C}$ iff $F\models\varphi \Leftrightarrow F\in\mathcal{C}$ for all $F$.
\end{definition}

Validity quantifies away the valuation and is therefore a property of $R$ alone; it is second order, being universal over all subsets of $W$.

\begin{definition}[Modal system]
A \emph{modal system} $S$ is a set of formulas, its theorems. $S$ is \emph{frame-sound} for $F$ if every theorem is valid on $F$; the \emph{frame class} of $S$ is the class of such $F$. $S$ \emph{proves reflection} (resp.\ \emph{the L\"ob axiom}) if $T(\varphi)$ (resp.\ $L(\varphi)$) is a theorem for all $\varphi$.
\end{definition}

Two systems recur as witnesses: the \emph{provability system}, whose theorems are the formulas valid on all transitive converse well-founded frames, and the \emph{self-sound system}, whose theorems are the formulas valid on the single reflexive point.

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:empty}
Every formula is valid on a frame with no worlds; hence every definable class contains the empty frame, and $\bot$ defines exactly the empty frames.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Validity is universal over worlds, vacuously true when there are none. Conversely $F\models\bot$ forces $W=\varnothing$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
No set of formulas defines the class of nonempty frames.
\end{corollary}

\section{Correspondence for the classical axioms}

Throughout, $p$ is a fixed variable and each correspondence uses one instance in that one variable. The pattern is uniform: to derive a relational property from validity one instantiates the \emph{minimal valuation} making the antecedent true.

\begin{theorem}[$T$ defines reflexivity]\label{thm:T}
$\Box p \to p$ is valid on $F$ iff $wRw$ for every $w$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Reflexivity makes the axiom immediate. Conversely fix $w$ and take $V(p):=\{x : wRx\}$; then $\Box p$ holds at $w$, so validity gives $w\in V(p)$, i.e.\ $wRw$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$4$ defines transitivity]
$\Box p\to\Box\Box p$ is valid on $F$ iff $R$ is transitive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Transitivity propagates $\Box p$ one step. Conversely $V(p):=\{x:wRx\}$ makes the antecedent true at $w$, and the conclusion says that every world reachable in two steps is reachable in one.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$D$ defines seriality]
$\neg\Box\bot$ is valid on $F$ iff every world has a successor. No propositional variable is needed.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[$B$ defines symmetry]
$p\to\Box\Diamond p$ is valid on $F$ iff $wRv$ implies $vRw$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Given $wRv$ take $V(p):=\{w\}$: the antecedent holds at $w$, hence $\Diamond p$ at $v$, producing $u$ with $vRu$ and $u=w$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[$5$ defines the euclidean property]
$\Diamond p \to \Box\Diamond p$ is valid on $F$ iff $wRv$ and $wRu$ imply $vRu$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Given $wRv$, $wRu$ take $V(p):=\{u\}$: then $\Diamond p$ holds at $w$, hence at $v$, supplying $z$ with $vRz$ and $z=u$.
\end{proof}

\section{The L\"ob correspondence}

\begin{definition}
$R$ is \emph{converse well-founded} if the reverse relation is well-founded; classically, iff every nonempty $S \subseteq W$ has an $R$-maximal element (some $a\in S$ with no $b\in S$ such that $aRb$); equivalently, iff there is no infinite chain $w_0Rw_1Rw_2\cdots$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Semantic L\"ob theorem]\label{thm:loebsound}
If $R$ is transitive and converse well-founded then $\Box(\Box\varphi\to\varphi)\to\Box\varphi$ is valid on $F$ for every $\varphi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Fix $V,w$ and assume the premise. Prove $\varphi$ at every successor $v$ of $w$ by induction along the well-founded reverse relation: the induction hypothesis gives $\varphi$ at every $t$ with $vRt$, those $t$ being successors of $w$ by transitivity, so $\Box\varphi$ holds at $v$; the premise at $v$ then yields $\varphi$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Transitivity is necessary]
If $L(p)$ is valid on $F$ then $R$ is transitive.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Let $wRv$ and $vRu$. Take
\[
  V(p) := \{x : wRx \text{ and } \forall y\,(xRy \Rightarrow wRy)\}.
\]
The premise $\Box(\Box p\to p)$ holds at $w$: if $z$ is a successor of $w$ all of whose successors satisfy $p$, then in particular they are successors of $w$, so $z\in V(p)$. Validity gives $p$ at $v$; the second conjunct applied to $u$ yields $wRu$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Converse well-foundedness is necessary]
If $L(p)$ is valid on $F$ then $R$ is converse well-founded.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose a nonempty $S$ has no $R$-maximal element, so each $a \in S$ has $b\in S$ with $aRb$. Pick $w\in S$ and set $V(p) := W\setminus S$. The premise holds at $w$: for $z$ with $wRz$, either $z\notin S$ and $p$ holds at $z$, or $z \in S$ and some successor of $z$ lies in $S$, falsifying $\Box p$ at $z$. Validity then gives $\Box p$ at $w$, i.e.\ no successor of $w$ lies in $S$ --- contradicting the choice of $b\in S$ with $wRb$.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
The maximal-element formulation keeps the argument choice-free: the ``no infinite ascending chain'' reading would require constructing an infinite sequence.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}[L\"ob defines the provability frames]\label{thm:loeb}
$F \models \Box(\Box p\to p)\to\Box p$ iff $R$ is transitive and converse well-founded.
\end{theorem}

\begin{corollary}[Irreflexivity]\label{cor:irrefl}
A frame validating the L\"ob axiom has no world seeing itself: the singleton $\{w\}$ would otherwise have no maximal element.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Joint inconsistency, semantic form]\label{thm:joint}
If $F$ validates both $L(p)$ and $T(p)$ then $F$ has no worlds.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Reflection forces reflexivity (Theorem~\ref{thm:T}); L\"ob forbids it (Corollary~\ref{cor:irrefl}).
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}
If a proof system proves both the reflection schema and the L\"ob schema, then every frame for which it is sound is empty: the frame-level shadow of the second incompleteness theorem.
\end{corollary}

\section{The finite collapse and the decidable bridge}

\begin{theorem}[Finite collapse]\label{thm:collapse}
Let $F$ have finitely many worlds. Then $F\models L(p)$ iff $R$ is transitive and irreflexive, i.e.\ iff $R$ is a strict partial order.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
One direction is Theorem~\ref{thm:loeb} with Corollary~\ref{cor:irrefl}. Conversely, a transitive irreflexive relation on a finite set is converse well-founded, since an infinite ascending chain would repeat a world and transitivity would then give $wRw$; Theorem~\ref{thm:loebsound} applies.
\end{proof}

Identify a frame on $\{0,\dots,n-1\}$ with its Boolean adjacency matrix $R\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$.

\begin{definition}
$R$ is a \emph{strict matrix} if $R_{ab}=R_{bc}=1 \Rightarrow R_{ac}=1$ for all $a,b,c$, and $R_{aa}=0$ for all $a$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[The bridge]\label{thm:bridge}
For every $n$ and every $R\in\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$, the frame of $R$ validates $\Box(\Box p\to p)\to\Box p$ if and only if $R$ is a strict matrix.
\end{theorem}

The left-hand side is universal over all valuations, i.e.\ over all subsets of the world set; the right-hand side is a check on $n^3+n$ entries. Without the finite collapse there would be no computation to perform, converse well-foundedness not being a finitary condition.

\section{Enumeration}

\begin{definition}
Let $\Lcount(n)$ be the number of matrices in $\{0,1\}^{n\times n}$ whose frame validates the L\"ob axiom, and $\Tcount(n)$ the number whose frame validates the reflection axiom.
\end{definition}

By Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge}, $\Lcount(n)$ is the number of labelled strict partial orders on $n$ points.

\begin{theorem}[Initial values]
$\Lcount(0)=1$, $\Lcount(1)=1$, $\Lcount(2)=3$, $\Lcount(3)=19$.
\end{theorem}

For $n=3$ the nineteen orders are: the empty order ($1$); the orders with exactly one comparable pair ($6$); the ``V'' and ``$\Lambda$'' shapes with one point below, respectively above, two incomparable points ($3+3$); and the six three-element chains. No configuration has exactly two comparabilities other than the V's, since a chain $i<j<k$ forces $i<k$: transitivity is what reduces the $2^{6}=64$ irreflexive relations on three points to $19$.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{Continuation.} Growing an order one point at a time --- choosing a downward-closed down-set $D$ and an upward-closed up-set $U$ with every element of $D$ below every element of $U$ --- gives
\[
  \Lcount(n) = 1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 19,\ 219,\ 4231,\ 130023,\ \dots
\]
the classical sequence of labelled partial orders. No closed form is known; the Kleitman--Rothschild theorem gives $\log_2 \Lcount(n) = n^2/4 + o(n^2)$.

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity]
$\Lcount(n)\le \Lcount(n+1)$ for all $n$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Adjoin an isolated world: extend $R$ by a zero last row and column. Transitivity and irreflexivity are preserved (any putative violating triple would have to involve the isolated world, which no arrow touches), and the map is injective since $R$ is recovered by restriction.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[The reflexive count]
$\Tcount(n)=2^{n^2-n}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:T}, validity of reflection says exactly that the $n$ diagonal entries are $1$; the remaining $n^2-n$ entries are free.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[L\"ob is rarer than reflection]
$\Lcount(3)=19 < 64 = \Tcount(3)$, out of $512$ frames on three worlds; and by Theorem~\ref{thm:joint} no nonempty frame is counted by both.
\end{theorem}

The gap widens without bound: $\Tcount(n)/2^{n^2}=2^{-n}$, whereas $\Lcount(n)/2^{n^2}=2^{-3n^2/4+o(n^2)}$.

\section{Transfer theory and the limits of definability}

\begin{definition}[Bounded morphism]
A \emph{bounded morphism} $f: F \to G$ is a map on worlds such that (\emph{forth}) $wRv$ implies $f(w)R^{G}f(v)$, and (\emph{back}) if $f(w)R^{G}u$ then there is $v$ with $wRv$ and $f(v)=u$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Truth lemma]\label{thm:truth}
For every bounded morphism $f:F\to G$, valuation $V$ on $G$, formula $\varphi$ and world $w$ of $F$:
\[
  G,V,f(w)\models\varphi \iff F, V\circ f, w \models \varphi .
\]
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on $\varphi$; for $\Box\varphi$, \emph{forth} gives one inclusion between the relevant successor sets and \emph{back} the other, so the two universal quantifications agree.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Transfer of validity]\label{cor:transfer}
If $f:F\to G$ is a surjective bounded morphism and $\varphi$ is valid on $F$, then $\varphi$ is valid on $G$. Consequently the frame class of every modal system is closed under surjective bounded morphic images.
\end{corollary}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{disjoint union} $F\sqcup G$ has as worlds the disjoint union of those of $F$ and $G$, with accessibility inherited within each summand and no arrows across.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:sum}
$F\sqcup G\models\varphi$ iff $F\models\varphi$ and $G\models\varphi$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Both injections are bounded morphisms (\emph{back} holds because no arrow crosses summands), so Theorem~\ref{thm:truth} identifies truth in the union at an injected world with truth in the summand; and every world of the union is injected.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Closure package]
For every modal system, the frame class is closed under surjective bounded morphic images, closed under disjoint unions, and reflects disjoint unions.
\end{corollary}

\begin{theorem}[Irreflexivity is not definable]\label{thm:irrefl-undef}
No set of modal formulas is valid exactly on the frames in which no world sees itself; hence no modal system has the irreflexive frames as its exact frame class.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
Let $F$ be the successor frame on $\mathbb{N}$, where $n$ sees exactly $n+1$; it is irreflexive. The constant map onto the single reflexive point is a surjective bounded morphism: \emph{forth} is trivial and \emph{back} holds since each $n$ has the successor $n+1$. By Corollary~\ref{cor:transfer} every formula valid on $F$ is valid on the loop, which is not irreflexive.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[``At least two worlds'' is not definable]
The two-world frame with no arrows maps onto the one-world frame with no arrows by a surjective bounded morphism, both clauses being vacuous.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Universality and ``some reflexive world'' are not definable]
``Every world sees every world'' holds on a single reflexive loop but fails on the disjoint union of two copies of it; ``some world is reflexive'' holds on the union of an irreflexive frame with a loop but fails on the irreflexive summand. Both contradict Theorem~\ref{thm:sum}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:irrefl-undef} is in instructive tension with Theorem~\ref{thm:loeb}: the L\"ob axiom defines a class all of whose members are irreflexive, yet irreflexivity by itself is undefinable. Modal formulas see only along arrows and cannot detect the identity of a world: a loop and an infinite forward ladder are modally indistinguishable.
\end{remark}

\begin{theorem}
A frame is sound for the provability system iff it is transitive and converse well-founded.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Soundness in one direction is Theorem~\ref{thm:loebsound} applied to each theorem. Conversely, a sound frame validates the L\"ob axiom in particular, and Theorem~\ref{thm:loeb} applies.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}
A frame is sound for the self-sound system iff its accessibility relation is equality: each world sees precisely itself.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The system proves $\Box p \to p$ and $p \to \Box p$, giving reflexivity and the fact that successors satisfy exactly what their source does; taking $V(p):=\{w\}$ excludes successors distinct from $w$. Conversely, if accessibility is equality then each world is the image of a bounded morphism from the single loop, so Corollary~\ref{cor:transfer} transports every theorem.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Dichotomy]
Both classes are nonempty --- the loop lies in the second, the empty frame and every finite strict order in the first --- and their intersection contains only empty frames.
\end{corollary}

\section{The degree monoid of a frame}

\begin{definition}
The \emph{$k$-fold reflection axiom} is $C_k(p) := \Box^k p \to p$; for $k=1$ it is the reflection axiom and for $k=0$ a tautology. Write $R^k$ for $k$-step reachability: $wR^kv$ iff there is a walk $w = x_0Rx_1R\cdots Rx_k = v$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:cycle}
$C_k(p)$ is valid on $F$ iff every world lies on a closed walk of length exactly $k$, i.e.\ $wR^kw$ for all $w$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Sufficiency is immediate. Conversely take $V(p):=\{x : wR^kx\}$; then $\Box^kp$ holds at $w$ by construction, so validity gives $wR^kw$. For $k=1$ this recovers Theorem~\ref{thm:T}.
\end{proof}

\begin{definition}[Degree monoid]
$D(F) := \{k\in\mathbb{N} : F\models\Box^kp\to p\}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}
$D(F)$ is an additive submonoid of $\mathbb{N}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}
$0\in D(F)$ via the empty walk. If $j,k\in D(F)$, concatenate a closed $j$-walk at $w$ with a closed $k$-walk at $w$ to obtain a closed $(j+k)$-walk; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:cycle}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[L\"ob frames]
If $F$ is nonempty and validates the L\"ob axiom then $D(F)=\{0\}$: a closed walk of positive length in a transitive relation would give $wRw$, contradicting Corollary~\ref{cor:irrefl}.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Equality frames]
If each world sees exactly itself then $D(F)=\mathbb{N}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cycle frames]
For the directed $n$-cycle $Z_n$, $D(Z_n) = n\mathbb{N}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Non-principality]\label{thm:k3}
Let $K_3$ be the three-world frame in which each world sees the other two and not itself. Then
\[
  D(K_3) = \{k : k \ne 1\} = \{0,2,3,4,5,\dots\} = \langle 2,3\rangle,
\]
and there is no $d$ with $D(K_3)=d\mathbb{N}$.
\end{theorem}
\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
There is no closed walk of length $1$ (no loops), one of length $2$ (out and back) and one of length $3$ (around the triangle); closure under addition supplies every $k\ge 4$. If $D(K_3)=d\mathbb{N}$ then $d\mid 2$ and $d\mid 3$, so $d=1$ and $1\in D(K_3)$, a contradiction.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:k3} refutes the natural conjecture that the graded soundness degrees of a frame are always the multiples of a fundamental period. The degree monoid is a numerical-semigroup-valued invariant: the depths at which a structure ``trusts itself'' are closed under addition but need not be closed under divisibility.
\end{remark}

\section{Algorithms}

\begin{algorithmbox}[L\"ob-validity check]
\emph{Input:} a Boolean matrix $R$ of size $n$. \emph{Output:} whether the frame validates the L\"ob axiom. Verify $R_{aa}=0$ for all $a$ and $R_{ab}\wedge R_{bc}\Rightarrow R_{ac}$ for all triples. Complexity $O(n^3)$, or $O(n^2)$ word operations with bitset rows. Correctness is Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge}; a naive semantic check would cost $O(2^n \cdot n \cdot |\varphi|)$ per formula and would not even be well defined for infinite frames.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Enumeration of labelled strict orders]
\emph{Input:} $n$. \emph{Output:} $\Lcount(n)$, or all L\"ob frames on $n$ worlds. Build up point by point: given a strict order $P$ on $\{0,\dots,m-1\}$, its extensions to $\{0,\dots,m\}$ are indexed by pairs $(D,U)$ with $D$ a down-set of $P$, $U$ an up-set of $P$, and every element of $D$ below every element of $U$ in $P$. These are precisely the conditions transitivity through the new point demands, and they force $D\cap U=\varnothing$ and hence irreflexivity. Cost is proportional to the number of orders produced times $4^{m}$ candidate pairs, far better than the $2^{n^2}$ of brute force.
\end{algorithmbox}

\begin{algorithmbox}[Degree monoid]
\emph{Input:} a matrix $R$ and a bound $B$. \emph{Output:} $D(F)\cap[0,B]$. Compute the sets $R^k(w)$ by iterated Boolean matrix--vector products and test $w \in R^k(w)$ for all $w$. Complexity $O(Bn^3)$. Once the truncation contains two coprime degrees $j,k$, all integers $\ge (j-1)(k-1)$ belong to $D(F)$.
\end{algorithmbox}

\section{Discussion}

\paragraph{What the census measures.} The identity $\Lcount(n) = \#\{\text{labelled strict partial orders on } n \text{ points}\}$ translates a second-order semantic condition into an order-theoretic one, licensed by Theorem~\ref{thm:collapse} and made effective by Theorem~\ref{thm:bridge}. ``A theory may not assert its own soundness'' becomes ``reflexive and irreflexive frames do not meet''; ``well-foundedness is a strong hypothesis'' becomes ``$19$ out of $512$, and $2^{-3n^2/4+o(n^2)}$ asymptotically''.

\paragraph{The role of the finite collapse.} Converse well-foundedness is indispensable in general: the strict order $<$ on $\mathbb{N}$ is transitive and irreflexive yet converse ill-founded, hence not a L\"ob frame. Transitivity plus irreflexivity is genuinely weaker over infinite carriers; the collapse is a finiteness phenomenon, and it is what makes the enumeration meaningful.

\paragraph{Definability has hard boundaries.} The closure principles are not technicalities: each is realised as an actual obstruction. Modal validity is invariant under operations preserving local visibility structure, and any property not so invariant --- however natural, and even if all frames of some definable class happen to have it --- is beyond axiomatic reach.

\paragraph{Degrees and semigroups.} The degree monoid connects the subject to numerical semigroups. Since $D(F)$ is the intersection over worlds of the closed-walk-length monoids of the digraph, the realisation problem is purely graph-theoretic.

\section{Future directions}

\begin{conjecture}[Realisation of degree monoids]
For every additive submonoid $S \le \mathbb{N}$ with $S\ne\{0\}$ and finite complement in the group it generates, there is a finite frame $F$ with $D(F)=S$; conversely every degree monoid of a finite frame is such a submonoid. The key insight is that $D(F)$ is the set of $k$ such that \emph{every} world lies on a closed walk of length $k$, so the question concerns the intersection over vertices of the cycle-length monoids of a digraph --- and $K_3$ already shows this intersection can be the non-principal semigroup $\langle 2,3\rangle$, refuting the naive ``always $d\mathbb{N}$'' reading. Two extremes ($\{0\}$, $\mathbb{N}$) and two nontrivial values ($n\mathbb{N}$, $\langle 2,3\rangle$) are established, so the general problem can be attacked with the closed-walk concatenation machinery already in hand.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[A Goldblatt--Thomason theorem for these frame classes]
A class $\mathcal{C}$ of finite frames is the frame class of some modal system iff $\mathcal{C}$ is closed under surjective bounded morphic images, closed under and reflecting disjoint unions, and closed under generated subframes. The three closure directions are established above, and they are strong enough to refute definability in three different ways (irreflexivity fails images, ``some reflexive world'' fails summands, non-emptiness fails the empty frame); the open half is the converse --- building, from a closed class, an explicit system (for instance the validity system of $\mathcal{C}$) and proving its frame class is exactly $\mathcal{C}$. The characterisation of the provability system's frame class is already such a converse for one class, so the pattern ``take the validity system of $\mathcal{C}$, show soundness for $\mathcal{C}$, and use a definability theorem for the reverse inclusion'' is available for generalisation.
\end{conjecture}

\begin{conjecture}[No modal shortcut for the counting sequence]
$\Lcount(n) = 1,1,3,19,219,4231,\dots$ is not expressible as $2^{q(n)}$ for a polynomial $q$, nor as any product of binomial coefficients; more sharply, for every fixed modal formula $\varphi$, the number of frames on $n$ labelled worlds validating $\varphi$ either has such a closed form or agrees with the labelled-poset sequence, with no intermediate growth rates achievable.
\end{conjecture}

\section{Conclusion}

Frame definability is the hinge between the syntax of modal axioms and the combinatorics of directed graphs. Turning it carefully, we found that the axiom expressing L\"ob's theorem pins down exactly the transitive converse well-founded frames; that over a finite world set this is exactly strict partial order; that the resulting census of L\"obian universes is the labelled-poset sequence $1,1,3,19,219,4231,130023,\dots$; that the rival axiom of internalised soundness admits $2^{n^2-n}$ frames and shares none of them; that three natural frame properties are provably beyond the expressive power of any axiom system; and that the graded degrees of self-trust form a numerical semigroup which need not be principal. On three worlds, the answer to the question with which we began is nineteen.

Counting the Frames of Provability: numerical demonstrations
============================================================

This self-contained script demonstrates, by explicit computation, the results of
the accompanying article and paper on frame definability for modal systems of
provability.

Background in one paragraph
---------------------------
A *frame* on the world set W is a binary relation R on W ("w can see v").  A
*valuation* assigns to each propositional variable the set of worlds where it is
true; satisfaction is the usual Kripke clause, with the box read as "at every
visible world".  A formula is *valid on a frame* when it is true at every world
under every valuation.  The central correspondences demonstrated here are:

  * The Loeb axiom  box(box p -> p) -> box p  is valid on F exactly when R is
    transitive and converse well-founded; on a finite frame this collapses to
    "transitive and irreflexive", i.e. R is a strict partial order.
  * The reflection axiom  box p -> p  is valid on F exactly when R is reflexive.
  * The n-fold reflection axiom  box^n p -> p  is valid on F exactly when every
    world lies on a closed walk of length exactly n.

Consequently the number of frames on n labelled worlds validating Loeb is the
number of labelled strict partial orders on n points: 1, 1, 3, 19, 219, 4231,
while the number validating reflection is 2^(n^2 - n).

Everything below is computed from scratch; no third-party packages are needed.

Run:  python3 demo.py
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# A frame on {0, ..., n-1} is stored as a tuple of n row-bitmasks:
# bit j of rows[i] is set iff i sees j.
Frame = Tuple[int, ...]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 0.  Basic predicates on frames
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_irreflexive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff no world sees itself."""
    return all(not (row >> i) & 1 for i, row in enumerate(rows))


def is_reflexive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff every world sees itself (validity of the reflection axiom)."""
    return all((row >> i) & 1 for i, row in enumerate(rows))


def is_transitive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff i sees j and j sees k implies i sees k."""
    n = len(rows)
    for i in range(n):
        row = rows[i]
        for j in range(n):
            if (row >> j) & 1 and (rows[j] & ~row) != 0:
                return False
    return True


def validates_loeb(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """Validity of the Loeb axiom on a *finite* frame: strict partial order."""
    return is_transitive(rows) and is_irreflexive(rows)


def validates_reflection(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """Validity of the reflection axiom box p -> p."""
    return is_reflexive(rows)


def all_frames(n: int) -> Iterable[Frame]:
    """Enumerate all 2^(n^2) frames on n labelled worlds."""
    full = 1 << n
    for rows in product(range(full), repeat=n):
        yield rows


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1.  Brute-force counts (small n) and the exact reflexive count
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def loeb_frame_count_bruteforce(n: int) -> int:
    """Count frames on n worlds validating Loeb, by exhaustive search."""
    return sum(1 for rows in all_frames(n) if validates_loeb(rows))


def reflexive_frame_count_bruteforce(n: int) -> int:
    """Count frames on n worlds validating reflection, by exhaustive search."""
    return sum(1 for rows in all_frames(n) if validates_reflection(rows))


def reflexive_frame_count_closed_form(n: int) -> int:
    """Closed form: fix the n diagonal entries, the other n^2-n are free."""
    return 1 << (n * n - n)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 2.  Fast enumeration of labelled strict partial orders
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Growing a poset one point at a time.  Suppose P is a strict partial order on
# {0,...,m-1} and we add the point m with strict down-set D (things below m) and
# strict up-set U (things above m).  The extension is again a strict partial
# order iff
#     (i)   D is downward closed in P,
#     (ii)  U is upward closed in P,
#     (iii) every element of D is below every element of U in P
#           (this is what transitivity through the new point demands, and it
#            forces D and U to be disjoint, hence irreflexivity).
# This yields an enumeration whose cost is proportional to the number of posets
# produced, rather than to 2^(n^2).


def extensions(rows: Frame) -> Iterable[Frame]:
    """All strict partial orders on m+1 points restricting to `rows` on m."""
    m = len(rows)
    down_closed: List[int] = []
    up_closed: List[int] = []
    universe = (1 << m) - 1
    for s in range(1 << m):
        # s is downward closed iff for every i in s, all predecessors of i are in s
        ok_down = True
        ok_up = True
        for i in range(m):
            if (s >> i) & 1:
                preds = sum(1 << j for j in range(m) if (rows[j] >> i) & 1)
                if preds & ~s:
                    ok_down = False
                succs = rows[i]
                if succs & ~s:
                    ok_up = False
            if not (ok_down or ok_up):
                break
        if ok_down:
            down_closed.append(s)
        if ok_up:
            up_closed.append(s)
    for d in down_closed:
        for u in up_closed:
            if d & u:
                continue
            # every element of D must already be below every element of U
            if any(
                (d >> i) & 1 and (rows[i] & u) != u
                for i in range(m)
            ):
                continue
            new_rows = []
            for i in range(m):
                r = rows[i]
                if (d >> i) & 1:  # i is below the new point m
                    r |= 1 << m
                new_rows.append(r)
            new_rows.append(u & universe)  # the new point sees exactly U
            yield tuple(new_rows)


def enumerate_posets(n: int) -> List[Frame]:
    """All labelled strict partial orders on {0,...,n-1}."""
    current: List[Frame] = [()]
    for _ in range(n):
        nxt: List[Frame] = []
        for p in current:
            nxt.extend(extensions(p))
        current = nxt
    return current


def loeb_frame_count(n: int) -> int:
    """The number of frames on n labelled worlds validating the Loeb axiom."""
    return len(enumerate_posets(n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 3.  Monotonicity: adjoining an isolated world
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def adjoin_isolated_world(rows: Frame) -> Frame:
    """Extend a frame on n worlds by one world that sees nothing and is unseen."""
    return tuple(rows) + (0,)


def check_monotonicity(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """The map 'adjoin an isolated world' injects Loeb frames on n into n+1."""
    small = enumerate_posets(n)
    big = set(enumerate_posets(n + 1))
    images = {adjoin_isolated_world(p) for p in small}
    injective = len(images) == len(small)
    return len(small), len(big), injective and images <= big


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 4.  Semantics: satisfaction and honest validity checking
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# We check validity of a formula on a small frame by brute force over all
# 2^(number of variables * n) valuations, so the bridge theorems below are
# tested semantically, not merely as matrix conditions.

Formula = object  # formulas are nested tuples, see below
# ('var', name) | ('bot',) | ('imp', a, b) | ('box', a)


def sat(rows: Frame, val: Dict[str, int], w: int, phi) -> bool:
    """Satisfaction of phi at world w; val maps a variable to a bitmask of worlds."""
    tag = phi[0]
    if tag == "bot":
        return False
    if tag == "var":
        return bool((val[phi[1]] >> w) & 1)
    if tag == "imp":
        return (not sat(rows, val, w, phi[1])) or sat(rows, val, w, phi[2])
    if tag == "box":
        return all(
            sat(rows, val, v, phi[1]) for v in range(len(rows)) if (rows[w] >> v) & 1
        )
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


def valid(rows: Frame, phi, variables: Sequence[str]) -> bool:
    """Validity of phi on the frame: all worlds, all valuations."""
    n = len(rows)
    for assignment in product(range(1 << n), repeat=len(variables)):
        val = dict(zip(variables, assignment))
        if not all(sat(rows, val, w, phi) for w in range(n)):
            return False
    return True


def box_iter(k: int, phi):
    """The formula box^k phi."""
    for _ in range(k):
        phi = ("box", phi)
    return phi


P = ("var", "p")
LOEB = ("imp", ("box", ("imp", ("box", P), P)), ("box", P))
REFLECTION = ("imp", ("box", P), P)
CONSISTENCY = ("imp", ("box", ("bot",)), ("bot",))  # not box bottom


def cycle_axiom(k: int):
    """The k-fold reflection axiom box^k p -> p."""
    return ("imp", box_iter(k, P), P)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 5.  The degree monoid of a frame
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def has_closed_walk(rows: Frame, k: int, w: int) -> bool:
    """True iff there is a walk of length exactly k from w back to w."""
    reach = {w}
    for _ in range(k):
        reach = {v for u in reach for v in range(len(rows)) if (rows[u] >> v) & 1}
    return w in reach


def degree_set(rows: Frame, bound: int = 12) -> List[int]:
    """Degrees k <= bound such that box^k p -> p is valid: every world on a k-walk."""
    return [
        k
        for k in range(bound + 1)
        if all(has_closed_walk(rows, k, w) for w in range(len(rows)))
    ]


def cycle_frame(n: int) -> Frame:
    """The directed n-cycle 0 -> 1 -> ... -> n-1 -> 0."""
    return tuple(1 << ((i + 1) % n) for i in range(n))


def complete_irreflexive_frame(n: int) -> Frame:
    """Every world sees every other world, and no world sees itself."""
    return tuple(sum(1 << j for j in range(n) if j != i) for i in range(n))


def equality_frame(n: int) -> Frame:
    """Each world sees exactly itself: n disjoint loops."""
    return tuple(1 << i for i in range(n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 6.  Bounded morphisms: why irreflexivity is not definable
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_bounded_morphism(src: Frame, tgt: Frame, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """f preserves accessibility (forth) and reflects it up to preimages (back)."""
    n, m = len(src), len(tgt)
    for w in range(n):
        for v in range(n):
            if (src[w] >> v) & 1 and not (tgt[f[w]] >> f[v]) & 1:
                return False  # forth fails
        for u in range(m):
            if (tgt[f[w]] >> u) & 1:
                if not any((src[w] >> v) & 1 and f[v] == u for v in range(n)):
                    return False  # back fails
    return True


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Reporting
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def rule(title: str) -> None:
    print()
    print("=" * 72)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 72)


def main() -> None:
    rule("1.  The bridge: semantic Loeb validity = strict partial order")
    print("For every frame on 3 worlds we compare")
    print("  (a) validity of  box(box p -> p) -> box p  over all 8^3 valuations")
    print("  (b) the matrix condition 'transitive and zero diagonal'.")

from __future__ import annotations

from itertools import product
from typing import Dict, FrozenSet, Iterable, List, Sequence, Set, Tuple

# A frame on {0, ..., n-1} is stored as a tuple of n row-bitmasks:
# bit j of rows[i] is set iff i sees j.
Frame = Tuple[int, ...]


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 0.  Basic predicates on frames
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_irreflexive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff no world sees itself."""
    return all(not (row >> i) & 1 for i, row in enumerate(rows))


def is_reflexive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff every world sees itself (validity of the reflection axiom)."""
    return all((row >> i) & 1 for i, row in enumerate(rows))


def is_transitive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff i sees j and j sees k implies i sees k."""
    n = len(rows)
    for i in range(n):
        row = rows[i]
        for j in range(n):
            if (row >> j) & 1 and (rows[j] & ~row) != 0:
                return False
    return True


def validates_loeb(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """Validity of the Loeb axiom on a *finite* frame: strict partial order."""
    return is_transitive(rows) and is_irreflexive(rows)


def validates_reflection(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """Validity of the reflection axiom box p -> p."""
    return is_reflexive(rows)


def all_frames(n: int) -> Iterable[Frame]:
    """Enumerate all 2^(n^2) frames on n labelled worlds."""
    full = 1 << n
    for rows in product(range(full), repeat=n):
        yield rows


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 1.  Brute-force counts (small n) and the exact reflexive count
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def loeb_frame_count_bruteforce(n: int) -> int:
    """Count frames on n worlds validating Loeb, by exhaustive search."""
    return sum(1 for rows in all_frames(n) if validates_loeb(rows))


def reflexive_frame_count_bruteforce(n: int) -> int:
    """Count frames on n worlds validating reflection, by exhaustive search."""
    return sum(1 for rows in all_frames(n) if validates_reflection(rows))


def reflexive_frame_count_closed_form(n: int) -> int:
    """Closed form: fix the n diagonal entries, the other n^2-n are free."""
    return 1 << (n * n - n)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 2.  Fast enumeration of labelled strict partial orders
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
#
# Growing a poset one point at a time.  Suppose P is a strict partial order on
# {0,...,m-1} and we add the point m with strict down-set D (things below m) and
# strict up-set U (things above m).  The extension is again a strict partial
# order iff
#     (i)   D is downward closed in P,
#     (ii)  U is upward closed in P,
#     (iii) every element of D is below every element of U in P
#           (this is what transitivity through the new point demands, and it
#            forces D and U to be disjoint, hence irreflexivity).
# This yields an enumeration whose cost is proportional to the number of posets
# produced, rather than to 2^(n^2).


def extensions(rows: Frame) -> Iterable[Frame]:
    """All strict partial orders on m+1 points restricting to `rows` on m."""
    m = len(rows)
    down_closed: List[int] = []
    up_closed: List[int] = []
    universe = (1 << m) - 1
    for s in range(1 << m):
        # s is downward closed iff for every i in s, all predecessors of i are in s
        ok_down = True
        ok_up = True
        for i in range(m):
            if (s >> i) & 1:
                preds = sum(1 << j for j in range(m) if (rows[j] >> i) & 1)
                if preds & ~s:
                    ok_down = False
                succs = rows[i]
                if succs & ~s:
                    ok_up = False
            if not (ok_down or ok_up):
                break
        if ok_down:
            down_closed.append(s)
        if ok_up:
            up_closed.append(s)
    for d in down_closed:
        for u in up_closed:
            if d & u:
                continue
            # every element of D must already be below every element of U
            if any(
                (d >> i) & 1 and (rows[i] & u) != u
                for i in range(m)
            ):
                continue
            new_rows = []
            for i in range(m):
                r = rows[i]
                if (d >> i) & 1:  # i is below the new point m
                    r |= 1 << m
                new_rows.append(r)
            new_rows.append(u & universe)  # the new point sees exactly U
            yield tuple(new_rows)


def enumerate_posets(n: int) -> List[Frame]:
    """All labelled strict partial orders on {0,...,n-1}."""
    current: List[Frame] = [()]
    for _ in range(n):
        nxt: List[Frame] = []
        for p in current:
            nxt.extend(extensions(p))
        current = nxt
    return current


def loeb_frame_count(n: int) -> int:
    """The number of frames on n labelled worlds validating the Loeb axiom."""
    return len(enumerate_posets(n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 3.  Monotonicity: adjoining an isolated world
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def adjoin_isolated_world(rows: Frame) -> Frame:
    """Extend a frame on n worlds by one world that sees nothing and is unseen."""
    return tuple(rows) + (0,)


def check_monotonicity(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int, bool]:
    """The map 'adjoin an isolated world' injects Loeb frames on n into n+1."""
    small = enumerate_posets(n)
    big = set(enumerate_posets(n + 1))
    images = {adjoin_isolated_world(p) for p in small}
    injective = len(images) == len(small)
    return len(small), len(big), injective and images <= big

# Part 4.  Semantics: satisfaction and honest validity checking
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------

def sat(rows: Frame, val: Dict[str, int], w: int, phi) -> bool:
    """Satisfaction of phi at world w; val maps a variable to a bitmask of worlds."""
    tag = phi[0]
    if tag == "bot":
        return False
    if tag == "var":
        return bool((val[phi[1]] >> w) & 1)
    if tag == "imp":
        return (not sat(rows, val, w, phi[1])) or sat(rows, val, w, phi[2])
    if tag == "box":
        return all(
            sat(rows, val, v, phi[1]) for v in range(len(rows)) if (rows[w] >> v) & 1
        )
    raise ValueError(f"unknown formula {phi!r}")


def valid(rows: Frame, phi, variables: Sequence[str]) -> bool:
    """Validity of phi on the frame: all worlds, all valuations."""
    n = len(rows)
    for assignment in product(range(1 << n), repeat=len(variables)):
        val = dict(zip(variables, assignment))
        if not all(sat(rows, val, w, phi) for w in range(n)):
            return False
    return True


def box_iter(k: int, phi):
    """The formula box^k phi."""
    for _ in range(k):
        phi = ("box", phi)
    return phi


P = ("var", "p")
LOEB = ("imp", ("box", ("imp", ("box", P), P)), ("box", P))
REFLECTION = ("imp", ("box", P), P)
CONSISTENCY = ("imp", ("box", ("bot",)), ("bot",))  # not box bottom


def cycle_axiom(k: int):
    """The k-fold reflection axiom box^k p -> p."""
    return ("imp", box_iter(k, P), P)


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 5.  The degree monoid of a frame
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def has_closed_walk(rows: Frame, k: int, w: int) -> bool:
    """True iff there is a walk of length exactly k from w back to w."""
    reach = {w}
    for _ in range(k):
        reach = {v for u in reach for v in range(len(rows)) if (rows[u] >> v) & 1}
    return w in reach


def degree_set(rows: Frame, bound: int = 12) -> List[int]:
    """Degrees k <= bound such that box^k p -> p is valid: every world on a k-walk."""
    return [
        k
        for k in range(bound + 1)
        if all(has_closed_walk(rows, k, w) for w in range(len(rows)))
    ]


def cycle_frame(n: int) -> Frame:
    """The directed n-cycle 0 -> 1 -> ... -> n-1 -> 0."""
    return tuple(1 << ((i + 1) % n) for i in range(n))


def complete_irreflexive_frame(n: int) -> Frame:
    """Every world sees every other world, and no world sees itself."""
    return tuple(sum(1 << j for j in range(n) if j != i) for i in range(n))


def equality_frame(n: int) -> Frame:
    """Each world sees exactly itself: n disjoint loops."""
    return tuple(1 << i for i in range(n))


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Part 6.  Bounded morphisms: why irreflexivity is not definable
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_bounded_morphism(src: Frame, tgt: Frame, f: Sequence[int]) -> bool:
    """f preserves accessibility (forth) and reflects it up to preimages (back)."""
    n, m = len(src), len(tgt)
    for w in range(n):
        for v in range(n):
            if (src[w] >> v) & 1 and not (tgt[f[w]] >> f[v]) & 1:
                return False  # forth fails
        for u in range(m):
            if (tgt[f[w]] >> u) & 1:
                if not any((src[w] >> v) & 1 and f[v] == u for v in range(n)):
                    return False  # back fails
    return True

def sat(rows: Frame, val: int, w: int, phi) -> bool:
    """Satisfaction at world w; `val` is a bitmask giving where p is true."""

    """Truth at every world under every valuation of the single variable p."""
    n = len(rows)

               for val in range(1 << n) for w in range(n))

def cond_reflexive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(sees(rows, i, i) for i in range(len(rows)))


def cond_transitive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    n = len(rows)
    return all(not (sees(rows, i, j) and sees(rows, j, k)) or sees(rows, i, k)
               for i in range(n) for j in range(n) for k in range(n))


def cond_serial(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    return all(rows[i] != 0 for i in range(len(rows)))


def cond_symmetric(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    n = len(rows)
    return all(not sees(rows, i, j) or sees(rows, j, i)
               for i in range(n) for j in range(n))


def cond_euclidean(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    n = len(rows)
    return all(not (sees(rows, i, j) and sees(rows, i, k)) or sees(rows, j, k)
               for i in range(n) for j in range(n) for k in range(n))


def cond_strict_order(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    return cond_transitive(rows) and not any(
        sees(rows, i, i) for i in range(len(rows)))


def cond_closed_walk(k: int) -> Callable[[Frame], bool]:
    def go(rows: Frame) -> bool:
        n = len(rows)
        for w in range(n):
            reach = {w}
            for _ in range(k):
                reach = {v for u in reach for v in range(n) if sees(rows, u, v)}
            if w not in reach:
                return False
        return True
    return go

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Sequence, Tuple

Frame = Tuple[int, ...]  # rows[i] is a bitmask: bit j set iff world i sees world j


def frame_from_pairs(n: int, edges: Sequence[Tuple[int, int]]) -> Frame:
    """Build a frame on n worlds from a list of arrows (i, j)."""
    rows: List[int] = [0] * n
    for i, j in edges:
        rows[i] |= 1 << j
    return tuple(rows)


def is_irreflexive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """No world sees itself."""
    return all(not (row >> i) & 1 for i, row in enumerate(rows))


def is_transitive(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """i sees j and j sees k implies i sees k, computed with bitset rows."""
    for i, row in enumerate(rows):
        for j in range(len(rows)):
            if (row >> j) & 1 and (rows[j] & ~row):
                return False
    return True


def validates_loeb(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff box(box p -> p) -> box p is valid on the frame, for every valuation.

    Correctness rests on the bridge theorem: on a finite frame, validity of the
    Loeb axiom is equivalent to the accessibility relation being a strict partial
    order.  The test therefore inspects O(n^3) triples (O(n^2) word operations
    with bitset rows) instead of quantifying over all 2^n valuations.
    """
    return is_transitive(rows) and is_irreflexive(rows)


def validates_reflection(rows: Frame) -> bool:
    """True iff box p -> p is valid: every world sees itself."""
    return all((row >> i) & 1 for i, row in enumerate(rows))

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import Iterable, List, Tuple

Frame = Tuple[int, ...]


def down_and_up_sets(rows: Frame) -> Tuple[List[int], List[int]]:
    """Bitmasks of the downward-closed and upward-closed subsets of the order."""
    m = len(rows)
    downs: List[int] = []
    ups: List[int] = []
    for s in range(1 << m):
        ok_down = True
        ok_up = True
        for i in range(m):
            if (s >> i) & 1:
                preds = sum(1 << j for j in range(m) if (rows[j] >> i) & 1)
                if preds & ~s:
                    ok_down = False
                if rows[i] & ~s:
                    ok_up = False
        if ok_down:
            downs.append(s)
        if ok_up:
            ups.append(s)
    return downs, ups


def extensions(rows: Frame) -> Iterable[Frame]:
    """All strict orders on m+1 points whose restriction to the first m is `rows`.

    Adding a point with down-set D and up-set U keeps the relation a strict
    partial order exactly when D is downward closed, U is upward closed, and
    every element of D already lies below every element of U.  The last
    condition is what transitivity through the new point demands; it forces
    D and U to be disjoint, hence irreflexivity.
    """
    m = len(rows)
    downs, ups = down_and_up_sets(rows)
    for d in downs:
        for u in ups:
            if d & u:
                continue
            if any((d >> i) & 1 and (rows[i] & u) != u for i in range(m)):
                continue
            new = [rows[i] | (1 << m) if (d >> i) & 1 else rows[i] for i in range(m)]
            new.append(u)
            yield tuple(new)


def enumerate_loeb_frames(n: int) -> List[Frame]:
    """All frames on n labelled worlds validating the Loeb axiom."""
    level: List[Frame] = [()]
    for _ in range(n):
        level = [q for p in level for q in extensions(p)]
    return level


def loeb_frame_count(n: int) -> int:
    """The census function: 1, 1, 3, 19, 219, 4231, 130023, ..."""
    return len(enumerate_loeb_frames(n))

from __future__ import annotations

from typing import List, Set, Tuple

Frame = Tuple[int, ...]


def step(rows: Frame, reach: Set[int]) -> Set[int]:
    """One application of the accessibility relation to a set of worlds."""
    return {v for u in reach for v in range(len(rows)) if (rows[u] >> v) & 1}


def has_closed_walk(rows: Frame, k: int, w: int) -> bool:
    """Is there a walk of exactly k arrows from w back to w?"""
    reach = {w}
    for _ in range(k):
        reach = step(rows, reach)
    return w in reach


def degree_monoid(rows: Frame, bound: int = 16) -> List[int]:
    """All k <= bound such that box^k p -> p is valid on the frame.

    By the graded correspondence theorem this holds exactly when every world
    lies on a closed walk of length exactly k.  The resulting set contains 0 and
    is closed under addition (concatenate walks), so it is an additive submonoid
    of the natural numbers; once the truncation exposes two coprime members j, k
    every integer >= (j-1)(k-1) belongs to it.  Cost: O(bound * n^2) word steps.
    """
    return [k for k in range(bound + 1)
            if all(has_closed_walk(rows, k, w) for w in range(len(rows)))]


def generators(degrees: List[int]) -> List[int]:
    """A minimal generating set of the numerical monoid spanned by `degrees`."""
    positive = [d for d in degrees if d > 0]
    gens: List[int] = []
    for d in positive:
        reachable = {0}
        for g in gens:
            reachable |= {r + g * t for r in list(reachable)
                          for t in range(1, d // g + 1)}
        if d not in reachable:
            gens.append(d)
    return gens

  switch(phi[0]){
    case 'bot': return false;
    case 'var': return !!val[w];
    case 'imp': return (!sat(M,val,w,phi[1])) || sat(M,val,w,phi[2]);
    case 'box':

  }
}
function valid(M, phi){
  for(let m=0;m<(1<<N);m++){

### A guided tour: from Löb's theorem to a census of finite universes

---

## 0 · The question

Here is a sentence that a mathematical theory can write about itself and cannot escape.

Write $\Box p$ for "$p$ is provable in this theory." In 1955 Martin Löb proved that if a
theory ever manages to prove *"if I can prove $p$, then $p$"*, then it already proves $p$
outright. As a schema:

$$\Box(\Box p \to p) \to \Box p.$$

Put $p := \bot$ and you have Gödel's second incompleteness theorem in one line: a
consistent theory cannot prove its own consistency. Modest self-trust is indistinguishable
from being wrong.

This page is about the *shape* of the universes in which that axiom holds, and about a
question with a startlingly concrete answer:

> **In how many small universes is the Löb axiom true?** On three worlds: exactly nineteen,
> out of 512.

Everything below builds up to that number and then goes past it. You can play at any point.

---

## 1 · Worlds, arrows, and the trick of forgetting the valuation

A **frame** is a set of *worlds* plus an *accessibility relation*: an arrow $w \to v$
meaning "from $w$, the world $v$ is visible." A **valuation** decides where each atomic
proposition is true. Formulas are then evaluated world by world, with one new clause:

$$\Box\varphi \text{ is true at } w \quad\text{iff}\quad \varphi \text{ is true at every world visible from } w.$$

The decisive move is to **forget the valuation**. A formula is *valid on a frame* when it
is true at every world under *every* valuation. Validity is therefore a property of the
arrows alone — pure combinatorics, all propositional content quantified away.

<details>
<summary>Why is "valid on a frame" a second-order condition? (click to reveal)</summary>

Because "every valuation" means "every assignment of a *subset of worlds* to each
variable." On a world set of size $n$ that is $2^n$ subsets per variable; on an infinite
world set it is a genuine quantification over the power set. That is what makes the
theorems below non-trivial: each one replaces this second-order quantifier with an
elementary condition on the relation. Background reading:
[Kripke semantics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kripke_semantics),
[modal correspondence theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Correspondence_theory_(modal_logic)).
</details>

**Try it now.** In the laboratory below, click cells of the $3\times3$ matrix to build a
universe. The verdicts are computed *semantically* — every valuation, every world — not by
any shortcut. Start with the preset "chain $0<1<2$", then delete the arrow $0\to2$ and
watch both transitivity and Löb collapse together.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

---

## 2 · Each axiom is a shape

The correspondences you just watched are theorems. Each is proved by finding the single
most stubborn valuation — the one that will break the axiom if the arrows misbehave.

| axiom | valid exactly when |
|---|---|
| $\Box p \to p$ (reflection) | every world sees itself |
| $\Box p \to \Box\Box p$ | the relation is transitive |
| $\neg\Box\bot$ (consistency) | every world sees something |
| $p \to \Box\Diamond p$ | the relation is symmetric |
| $\Diamond p \to \Box\Diamond p$ | any two worlds seen from a common world see each other |

<details>
<summary>The one-line proof for reflection (click to reveal)</summary>

Fix a world $w$ and take the valuation "$p$ is true exactly at the worlds $w$ can see."
Then $\Box p$ is true at $w$ by construction. If the axiom is valid, $p$ must be true at
$w$ too — and by the definition of the valuation, that says precisely $w R w$. The
converse is immediate. Notice that a *single instance* over a *single variable* already
does all the work; a richer language is never needed.
</details>

Don't take the table on faith. This demonstration checks every axiom against its predicted
relational condition on **every** frame with at most three worlds — all $1 + 2 + 16 + 512$
of them — and reports perfect agreement:

{{demo:1}}

## 3 · The deep case: what Löb asks of a universe

> **Theorem.** A single instance of $\Box(\Box p \to p) \to \Box p$ is valid on a frame
> exactly when the accessibility relation is **transitive** and **converse well-founded**:
> there is no infinite chain $w_0 \to w_1 \to w_2 \to \cdots$.

<details>
<summary>Proof sketch, both directions (click to reveal)</summary>

**Sufficiency.** Assume transitivity and converse well-foundedness, fix a valuation, and
assume the premise $\Box(\Box p\to p)$ at $w$. Prove $p$ at every successor by induction
running *backwards* along the relation — converse well-foundedness is exactly the licence
to do that. At a successor $v$, the induction hypothesis gives $p$ at everything $v$ sees
(which transitivity says $w$ also sees), so $\Box p$ holds at $v$, and the premise
delivers $p$.

**Necessity of transitivity.** Use the valuation
$x \mapsto$ "$w$ sees $x$, and everything $x$ sees is also seen by $w$."
It makes the premise true at $w$ for free, and the conclusion at a successor $v$ says
exactly that $v$'s successors are $w$'s successors.

**Necessity of converse well-foundedness.** Suppose some nonempty set $S$ has no maximal
element, i.e. each of its worlds sees another of its worlds. Interpret $p$ as "*not* in
$S$." Then the premise holds throughout $S$ (each $z \in S$ has a successor in $S$, which
falsifies $\Box p$ at $z$ vacuously) while the conclusion fails. Note the craft here: by
using "every nonempty set has a maximal element" instead of "no infinite chain," the
argument never *builds* an infinite sequence, so it needs no choice principle at all.
</details>

Two consequences fall out immediately.

* **A Löb frame is irreflexive**: a world seeing itself is an infinite ascending chain all
  by itself.
* **The joint inconsistency**: no *nonempty* frame validates both $\Box p \to p$ and the
  Löb axiom. Reflection demands that every world see itself; Löb forbids it. Gödel's second
  theorem, as a collision between two graph conditions.

Verify this yourself in the laboratory above: no matter what you click, the "reflection"
and "Löb" badges never light up together unless you empty the frame of arrows *and*
that still fails reflection. There is no escape.

---

## 4 · The collapse that makes counting possible

Converse well-foundedness talks about infinite chains — hardly a finite check. But on a
*finite* frame an infinite chain must repeat a world, and repeating a world in a transitive
relation makes a loop. So:

> **Finite collapse.** On a frame with finitely many worlds, the Löb axiom is valid exactly
> when the relation is transitive and irreflexive — that is, exactly when it is a
> [**strict partial order**](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partially_ordered_set).

This is the hinge of the whole story: a statement quantifying over all valuations becomes a
scan of $n^3$ triples. The algorithm below is the resulting decision procedure.

{{algorithm:0}}

<details>
<summary>Why the collapse is genuinely a finiteness phenomenon (click to reveal)</summary>

Transitive and irreflexive is strictly weaker than the Löb condition on infinite frames.
Take the usual strict order $<$ on the natural numbers: transitive, irreflexive, and yet
$0 < 1 < 2 < \cdots$ is an infinite ascending chain, so it is *not* converse well-founded
and the Löb axiom fails on it. Finiteness is exactly what rules such frames out.
</details>

---

## 5 · The census

Now we can count. A frame on $n$ labelled worlds is an $n \times n$ matrix of bits, so
there are $2^{n^2}$ of them; validating Löb means being a labelled strict partial order.

$$1,\ 1,\ 3,\ 19,\ 219,\ 4231,\ 130023,\ \dots$$

Brute force dies quickly ($6.9\times10^{10}$ matrices at $n = 6$). The enumeration
algorithm below grows every order one point at a time instead, and produces the whole
census in seconds:

{{algorithm:1}}

Here is the census made visible, against the rival count $2^{n^2-n}$ of frames validating
the reflection axiom:

{{visualization:0}}

The asymmetry is the punchline. **Trust is cheap**: fixing the diagonal costs a factor
$2^{-n}$, so reflexive frames are always a healthy exponential slice. **Well-foundedness is
rare**: the labelled-poset count is $2^{n^2/4 + o(n^2)}$, a vanishing sliver of the
$2^{n^2}$ frames. On three worlds the tally is stark — **64 validate reflection, 19
validate Löb, 0 validate both.**

And here are all nineteen, drawn:

{{visualization:1}}

<details>
<summary>Why nineteen, and not sixty-four? (click to reveal)</summary>

There are $2^6 = 64$ irreflexive relations on three labelled points, but transitivity
prunes them to $19$: the empty order ($1$), the orders with exactly one comparable pair
($6$), the "V" and "$\Lambda$" shapes with one point below or above two incomparable
points ($3+3$), and the six three-element chains. Nothing else survives, because a chain
$i<j<k$ is *forced* to contain $i<k$. Transitivity is not a free constraint — it is the
whole difference between $64$ and $19$.

One pleasant regularity: adjoining a world that sees nothing and is seen by nothing turns
a Löb frame on $n$ worlds into one on $n+1$ worlds, injectively. So the census is monotone;
doubt-friendly universes never become scarcer as you add room.
</details>
